explain.say: In the 1920s a few blocks of upper Manhattan became the capital of Black America. Writers, painters and jazz musicians gathered in Harlem, and the philosopher Alain Locke announced a New Negro, using the word of the time: proud, modern and free. The web shows the people and ideas of the Harlem Renaissance.

explain.say: Why Harlem, and why then? Look at the map. From about 1910, millions of Black Americans left the rural South, escaping segregation laws and lynching, for work in northern cities like New York and Chicago. Historians call it the Great Migration. What happens to art when so many people with shared memories arrive in one place?

draw.label: The Great Migration: millions of Black Americans left the rural South for northern cities

explain.say: Look at the four rivers. In 1921, still a teenager, Langston Hughes published The Negro Speaks of Rivers, in which one voice remembers the Euphrates, the Congo, the Nile and the Mississippi, a soul grown deep like the rivers. Later he wrote poems in the rhythms of jazz and blues. Why might a young poet claim such a long history?

draw.label: The four rivers of Langston Hughes’s 1921 poem, from the ancient world to America

explain.say: Now Zora Neale Hurston's 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. Follow Janie through three marriages: an older farmer, a man who becomes mayor and silences her, and Tea Cake, with whom she finds joy, until a hurricane brings tragedy. Hurston writes the talk in the Black Southern speech she recorded as an anthropologist. Why does voice matter so much here?

explain.say: Two roads to a Black voice: Hughes, the poet of the city and the blues; Hurston, the novelist of Southern folk life. Hurston died poor in 1960, nearly forgotten, until the novelist Alice Walker found her unmarked grave and wrote about her in 1975. Wonderful work. Challenge: read a Hughes poem aloud with a blues rhythm in mind.

faq.a: A flowering of African American literature, music, art and ideas centred on Harlem, New York, from about 1918 to the mid-1930s. Writers like Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay and Countee Cullen asserted Black pride and creativity.
asks: What is the Harlem Renaissance known for?

faq.q: What is The Negro Speaks of Rivers about?
faq.a: Hughes's short 1921 poem gives one voice to the whole history of Black people, linking ancient rivers of Africa and the Middle East with the Mississippi, to claim a deep, dignified heritage.

faq.q: Why is Their Eyes Were Watching God written in dialect?
faq.a: Hurston, a trained anthropologist, valued the speech of Black Southern communities as rich and poetic. Writing dialogue in that idiom celebrates it, while the narration uses standard English, and Janie's finding her own voice is the novel's theme.
The movement of about six million Black Americans from the rural South to cities in the North, Midwest and West between about 1910 and 1970, escaping segregation and violence and seeking work.
asks: Why did Black Americans move north?

faq.a: Alice Walker, author of The Color Purple, searched for Hurston's unmarked grave in Florida in 1973 and published an essay about her in Ms. magazine in 1975, sparking a revival of her work.
asks: Alice Walker and Zora Neale Hurston

facts: Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro was published in 1925.
Langston Hughes's The Negro Speaks of Rivers first appeared in 1921 in The Crisis, the magazine edited by W. E. B. Du Bois.
Zora Neale Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God was published in 1937.
